reasoning: The disagreement centers entirely on the .nvchecker.toml file. Qwen flagged it as unsafe because it fetches version data from a Google Cloud Run URL. However, .nvchecker.toml is a configuration file for maintainer tooling (nvchecker) used to check for upstream updates. It is not executed during makepkg (build/install) and does not affect the integrity of the packaged binaries, which are pinned with SHA256 checksums in the PKGBUILD. Per the threat model, development tooling not referenced by PKGBUILD functions is out of scope. The actual packaging files are safe and standard.
disagreement_analysis: Qwen incorrectly classified .nvchecker.toml as a supply-chain risk. It conflated a maintainer version-checking configuration with an actual source fetch in the PKGBUILD. Deepseek correctly identified it as standard maintainer tooling and marked it safe.
false_positives: Qwen's flag on .nvchecker.toml: This is a version-checking config for maintainer tooling (nvchecker), not executed during makepkg. The PKGBUILD itself uses pinned checksums from the official upstream source, so there is no injection risk here.
learnings: Models must distinguish between source fetching in the PKGBUILD (which affects build integrity) and version-checking configurations like .nvchecker.toml (which are maintainer tooling).
Reinforce the rule that development tooling, CI scripts, and maintainer configs in the source tree are out of scope unless explicitly sourced or executed by PKGBUILD functions or .install scripts.
